articles.title: Oleksandr Usyk is considering a return to cruiserweight, casting Tyson Fury's hopes of a trilogy fight into doubt
articles.summary: Oleksandr Usyk is planning to return to boxing next year, but is considering moving back down to cruiserweight; Tyson Fury had been gunning for a trilogy fight with Usyk after his clash with Anthony Joshua; Usyk has been the undisputed champion at both heavyweight and cruiserweight before
articles.body:
The great Ukrainian, an Olympic gold medallist, has been an undisputed champion twice over at heavyweight and prior to that also at cruiserweight.

After beating Rico Verhoeven in their WBC title fight in Egypt earlier this year, Usyk, unbeaten as a professional, vacated the titles he held.

He is anticipating returning to boxing, but could do so back down at cruiserweight.

"Usyk has already cleaned out the heavyweight division. Now he is considering a return to cruiserweight, his natural weight class, to make history again," Serhii Lapin, CEO of Usyk's promotional company Ready To Fight, told Sky Sports .

"He loves challenges, and this could be the next one he'd like to take on."

The possibility of Usyk moving down in weight casts into doubt a third fight with Tyson Fury. Britain's Fury has boxed Usyk twice before. He lost both bouts but has publicly criticised the judge's decision in his second fight with Usyk and called for a third.

Fury wants to box Usyk after his December mega-fight with Anthony Joshua, but the Ukrainian might be considering facing new opponents now.

If he wants to go undisputed yet again at 200lbs, he would have to target imposing champion David Benavidez, who fights Michal Cieslak for the WBC, WBO and WBA cruiserweight belts on December 5.

articles.title: Volkanovski se sincera sobre lo que le queda en las MMA antes de retirarse
articles.standfirst: El campeón de peso pluma no tiene pensado realizar muchos más combates a sus 38 años, por lo que busca enfrentarse a grandes nombres y cobrar un buen cheque
articles.summary: El campeón de peso pluma no tiene pensado realizar muchos más combates a sus 38 años, por lo que busca enfrentarse a grandes nombres y cobrar un buen cheque
articles.body: Alexander Volkanovski es uno de los peleadores más grandes que han pasado por la UFC. El GOAT del peso pluma viene de agrandar aún más su legado el pasado UFC 333 tras finalizar a Movsar Evloev, y ha declarado que su intención es subir a peso ligero a por el doble cinturón dejando vacante su título en las 145 libras. El motivo es simple, ya que a sus 38 años sabe que le quedan pocas balas en la recámara y quiere aprovecharlas al máximo. Hay pocas cosas que le queden por cumplir a Volkanovski en su carrera, pero una de ellas es esa doble corona. En una entrevista con Ariel Helwani, el peleador australiano ha dejado claro que a día de hoy lo único que busca es un buen cheque ante un rival de renombre, puesto que quiere preservar su físico y retirarse antes de que el deporte le retire a él. "¿Por qué hago esto? Obviamente, por el sueldo. Nunca más recibiré un sueldo como este, pero quiero cuidar mi salud y estar ahí para mis hijos. Estoy satisfecho con lo que he hecho, tengo la suerte de ser un peleador que ya no necesita hacer esto. Me tomo cada combate tal y como viene", afirmó 'The Great'. En los últimos días ha propuesto varias opciones a la UFC. Una pelea de retiro ante Justin Gaethje por el cinturón de peso ligero, un combate ante Arman Tsarukyan por el título vacante de peso ligero en caso de que Gaethje se retire, e incluso una revancha ante Ilia Topuria. Volkanovski sabe que en peso pluma no hay nombres tan mediáticos, por lo que sus últimos combate quiere que sean en una categoría donde cobre más dinero al enfrentarse a un peleador de renombre. Además, la cabeza es algo muy importante para él, por lo que no quiere prolongar su carrera demasiado antes de recibir un K.O. que le produzca daños irreparables. "Las lesiones en el resto del cuerpo no me preocupan, pero en lo que respecta a la cabeza no quiero arriesgarme. Un golpe fuerte en el cerebro, una conmoción cerebral y se acabó. Así es como lo veo. Estoy sopesando todas esas opciones", finalizó.

articles.title: Canelo Alvarez vs. Christian Mbilli Judges' Scorecards, Punch Stats and Prize Money
articles.summary: Canelo Alvarez is once again world champion after a unanimous decision win over Christian Mbilli to win the WBC super middleweight title at Kingdom Arena in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.
articles.body:
Canelo Alvarez is once again world champion after a unanimous decision win over Christian Mbilli to win the WBC super middleweight title at Kingdom Arena in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

Canelo got off to a strong start in the opening round. He didn't indulge in an all-out fire fight, but he won the technical exchanges in the first. Mbilli also let his hands go and scored on a few punches himself. It didn't take long for Mbilli to settle in, though. He picked up the pace in the second round and showed he might be able to steal some rounds.

Mbilli did a good job of making the early rounds competitive. Canelo wasn't able to pull ahead early in the bout, but he appeared to turn the tide as the bout reached the middle rounds.

Canelo opened up his repertoire in the sixth round with some hard counters to both the body and the head.

Mbilli's pace was an issue for much of the night. His best bet was to swarm the challenger, but he allowed Alvarez to set the pace.

Some controversy came into play in Round 8. Alvarez was dipping his head, but it was Mbilli who had a point deducted by the referee for punching him behind the head.

It was a break that Canelo didn't really need. As the fight wore on, Alvarez's experience and technical advantages became clearer. He pulled away on the scorecards and didn't look back.

Mbilli turned in a disappointing performance, but it did appear that he might have suffered an arm injury.

Regardless, Canelo wasn't truly pushed in the fight and wound up adding another championship performance to his resume.

Saturday was the first time we had seen Canelo in the ring since his loss to Terence Crawford in September 2025. Crawford took the undisputed titles, but was stripped of one and dropped the rest upon his retirement.

That opened the door for Alvarez to once again claim a championship that has been familiar to him for much of his career.

It also begs the question of what's next for him. He's 36 years old with 69 professional fights under his belt. Retirement talk is bound to creep in after every fight he has over the next few years.

To hear him tell it, he's got a few more big appearances in him, though. He knows there aren't a ton of years left, but he's also comfortable with what he's accomplished in the sport.

"If it were up to me, it would never be enough. But I think four or five more fights would be enough. I've already done everything I needed to do in boxing. I've done more than I ever imagined I would," he told Brett Okamoto of ESPN.

Alvarez still clearly has the draw to generate plenty of money. He reportedly made $47 million off the fight while Mbilli was paid $9 million.

There are still some interesting fights out there for him. A rematch against Dmitry Bivol would be a massive attraction for the sport. Canelo came up short in his bid for the light heavyweight title in 2022, but Bivol still holds those titles with recent wins over Artur Beterbiev and Michael Eifert.

Either way fans, should enjoy Canelo's fights while they still can and he's fighting at a championship level.

articles.title: Canelo Alvarez returns to beat Christian Mbilli and reclaim WBC super-middleweight world championship in Riyadh
articles.summary: Canelo Alvarez outscores Christian Mbilli to win back WBC title in Riyadh; Jaime Munguia came close to disaster but retained the WBA super-middleweight title, beating Nikita Zon; Watch Chris Billam-Smith fight Cheavon Clarke on November 7 live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
The Mexican superstar won the title beating Mbilli by unanimous decision in Riyadh.

Canelo was returning to boxing a year after his stunning loss to Terence Crawford and went straight in with a strong, previously undefeated world champion.

Mbilli did press Alvarez in the first half of the fight. He threw in busy bursts and moved Canelo into the ropes.

But Canelo began to exert increasing control of the action from the sixth round onwards.

With brilliant skill he used a right uppercut to open a path for a hard right cross. He grew more comfortable on the ropes, working with counter-punches, and his vicious uppercut made Mbilli wary.

In the eighth round Canelo finished a four-punch combination with a right to the head. Mbilli drove forward and all of a sudden the referee took a point off the champion for hitting round the back of the head.

Mbilli urgently needed to shift momentum. Instead Canelo turned the screw. Alvarez came off the ropes to work from the centre of the ring, drilling Mbilli with his right hook.

In the final round Mbilli struck in a good shot but backed off. Canelo even waved him in again, but Mbilli wouldn't respond.

Canelo pressed forward, and Mbilli smacked him with a hard right. Canelo wanted to finish fighting and blasted home an excellent right.

He made sure of a unanimous decision, taking the win 115-112, 116-111 and 117-110 on the cards.

Alvarez is a vastly experienced veteran, who's won it all many times over in his 68-bout professional career. Yet he was delighted, almost relieved to be a world champion again.

"It's so difficult to explain. It's something unbelievable," Canelo said. "Now after 21 years as a professional, 16 years ago I won my first title, now I won the title again… I want to thank everybody back home.

"I knew he was a strong fighter. He didn't throw a lot of punches because it's difficult to throw punches with me... I did perfectly," he added.

"I'm going to keep learning, I'm going to keep working hard. I'm going to take a couple of weeks off and then come back."

Jaime Munguia had to weather an almighty scare to carve out a unanimous decision win over Nikita Zon and defend his WBA super-middleweight title.

Zon, genuinely an awkward southpaw, found a home for heavy backhand lefts in the opening rounds. He drove Munguia to the ropes and into corners.

He was on the verge of knocking out Munguia in the sixth round. He led with a long left uppercut, badly hurting the Mexican. Munguia retreated but Zon swarmed all over him. He hammered Munguia but the champion refused to fall.

When Zon tired, Munguia hit back and he took clear control in the late rounds to win 16-112 and 117-111 twice on the scorecards.

Towering featherweight Rafael Espinoza easily dismissed replacement opponent Ricardo Blandon to retain the WBO world title.

He banged a flush cross into the top of the Nicaraguan's head which opened up a nasty cut along Blandon's eyelid. The ringside doctor pulled him out in the third round immediately after inspecting it.

The event goes down inside the familiar META APEX in Las Vegas, Nevada. Our main event on this Halloween event is Renato Moicano vs. Tom Nolan ( see betting odds here ).

It feels a little odd to see a UFC fight night land on Halloween. It would be nice if UFC did something to dress up for the occasion, but knowing them it will probably be business as usual.

Renato Moicano vs. Tom Nolan draw the short straw of being unable to go trick or treating with their kids this night ( are you? ). They are meeting in the main event, despite Moicano saying he was desperate to escape the APEX.

articles.title: UFC Vegas 123 video: Julian Erosa retires after wild 91-second comeback knockout
articles.summary: Julian Erosa said goodbye to MMA with a "fairytale" comeback knockout win in his UFC Vegas 123 retirement bout.
articles.body:
Julian Erosa ended his MMA career on a spectacular high at UFC Fight Night 292 when he rallied to knock out JeongYeong Lee.

After Lee (11-4 MMA, 2-3 UFC) stormed out of the gate and cracked Erosa (31-13 MMA, 10-9 UFC) with a huge punch and nearly finished the job inside the first minute, the veteran survived and slowed down the action. He quickly got back in the firefight, but Erosa was on the one to seal the deal as he dropped his foe with a clean shot then put him out cold with ground shots at the 1:31 mark of Round 1 on Saturday at Meta APEX in Las Vegas.

Check out the replay of the amazing moment below (via X ):

Moments before the knockout, UFC Hall of Famer Daniel Cormier questioned Erosa's decision to stand and trade. He was quickly silenced by Erosa, though, and called it a "fairytale" moment after seeing Lee put out cold

The 37-year-old Erosa had three stints under the UFC banner. He said now was the time to lay down the gloves, though, as he shared his retirement interview alongside his wife and child.

"I feel so amazing," Erosa said in his post-fight interview with Cormier. "" knew this was going to be my last fight, so I wanted to go out with a bang. I want to do this tomorrow, but I had to make the decision that was going to be my last fight, win, lose or draw. And I'm happy with that."

articles.title: Mbilli vs Alvarez: Saul 'Canelo' Alvarez reclaims world title with vintage performance
articles.summary: Saul 'Canelo' Alvarez reclaims the WBC super-middleweight title with a vintage performance against Christian Mbilli in Riyadh.
articles.body:
Saul 'Canelo' Alvarez reclaimed the WBC super-middleweight title with a vintage performance against Christian Mbilli in Riyadh.

Just over one year since losing his belts to Terance Crawford, Mexican pound-for-pound great Alvarez returned to action with a confident victory by unanimous decision.

The 36-year-old, in his 69th professional fight, showed trademark slick defence and counter punching as he outclassed Mbilli to win 115–112, 116–111, 117–110 on the judges' scorecards.

It was the 64th victory of four-weight world champion Alvarez's illustrious career, while 31-year-old Mbilli suffered his first defeat in 31 bouts.

"It's so difficult to explain," said Alvarez.

"It's something unbelievable, this feeling. Like my first title. Thirty-one years as a professional. Sixteen years ago, I won my first title. Now, I won the title again. I'm so proud."

Doubts had been raised in recent weeks about whether the event could safely go ahead due to the growing conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthi movement.

Just two days before the fight, Saudi Press Agency reported the Civil Defence had intercepted two ballistic missiles over Riyadh.

Earlier in October, a missile strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.

While other sporting events in Saudi Arabia - including The Six Kings Slam tennis exhibition, the final round of the 2026 World Rally Championship and the 2026 Urban Cycling World Championships - have been cancelled, the combat sports world has not followed suit.

Cameroon-born Mbilli, who trains in Canada, was making the first defence of his WBC title after being elevated to champion in January.

Alvarez, meanwhile, was competing for the first time without a world title to his name since 2015.

Pundits had questioned whether Alvarez's skills were declining following defeat by Crawford and over a year out of the ring, but his response was emphatic.

Mbilli pressured Alvarez in the early stages, peppering him against the ropes, with the Mexican looking to land big counters.

Alvarez responded by dismissively shaking his head to shrug off their impact, before goading Mbilli into attacking again.

Although Mbilli was throwing more punches, it was Alvarez who was landing the harder shots, with a couple of big right uppercuts finding the mark in round six.

The pattern continued in the next few rounds, with Alvarez countering the busy but largely ineffective Mbilli, before the defending champion was dealt a further blow by being docked a point for hits to the back of the head.

From there Alvarez cruised to the finish line with Mbilli continuing to push forward but posing little threat to the Mexican.

Alvarez's defence and timing of punches was too slick throughout, and although Mbilli landed a couple of stinging right hands in the closing stages, it was in vain.

Alvarez did not mention who he wants to fight next in his post-fight interview, but hinted at a quick return to training.

"I'm going to rest. I'm going to keep learning. I'm going to keep working hard," said Alvarez.

"And right now I'm going to be a couple of weeks off and then come back."

articles.title: 'Phenomenal:' Jake Paul, Terence Crawford and more react to Canelo Alvarez's vintage win over Christian Mbilli
articles.summary: Saul "Canelo" Alvarez turned back the clock Saturday night — and the boxing world took notice.
articles.body:
Saul "Canelo" Alvarez turned back the clock Saturday night, and the boxing world took notice.

The Mexican superstar returned from a 13-month layoff to defeat Christian Mbilli by unanimous decision and reclaim the WBC super middleweight championship in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. Alvarez delivered a vintage performance, using his experience, aggression and precision punching to get the better of the previously unbeaten Mbilli.

The victory marked Alvarez's first fight since losing to Terence Crawford in September 2025 , a defeat that raised questions about how much the 36-year-old former two-time undisputed champion had left in the tank.

Those questions received a strong answer Saturday, as Alvarez earned his first victory in more than a year and improved his professional record to 64-3-2 (39 KOs).

Among those reacting to the result was Jake Paul, who praised Alvarez's performance while once again teasing a potential fight between the two.

"Out of the ring for 13 months but still the same old Canelo. Respect," Paul wrote on social media. "Did take a lot of punches though. We will dance my friend, we will dance."

Paul and Alvarez were previously linked to a potential blockbuster boxing match before Alvarez signed a lucrative deal with Turki Alalshikh's Riyadh Season in 2025.

Other observers were similarly impressed with the veteran's showing. One reaction, from former British boxer, promoter and analyst David Coldwell, summed up the fight accurately and succinctly in just three words: "Old manned him."

articles.title: It takes a village: How Manisha Bhanwala rose from Siwaha's narrow lanes to top of the world
articles.summary: JIND: In India, villages make champions. Daughters of the soil, sons too, emerging from all corners, remote and close, carrying the dreams of a nation.
articles.body: JIND: In India, villages make champions. Daughters of the soil, sons too, emerging from all corners, remote and close, carrying the dreams of a nation. For Manisha Bhanwala, that journey began in Siwaha, a village in Haryana's Jind district, the narrow lanes of which now lead to the doorstep of a world champion. Late on Friday in Kazakhstan's Astana, Manisha became India's first-ever woman world champion in wrestling, that ancient Indian sport.Despite its proximity to the Capital, locating Siwaha - a modest village with around 4,500 registered voters - can prove a challenge. The routemap app, a global go-to, probably found its Everest in trying to locate it once the vehicle turned off the Jind-Panipat highway. A million reroutes later, once inside the village, there was no need for navigation. Ask anyone for the world champion's house, and enthusiastic children or youngsters on motorbikes happily escorted you to her doorstep. The modest two-storey house, tucked inside a narrow lane, has become a landmark.Outside, Manisha's maternal uncle Nanha sat on a tractor, tending to the family's cattle in between entertaining the frequent stream of visitors. After a quick request to secure the family dog, we were escorted inside to find Manisha's mother, Meena Devi, and uncle, wrestling coach Vinod Kumar, soaking in the moment on a charpai."It feels as though everything has suddenly changed. Before her world championship triumph, hardly anyone visited our home," Meena says simply, the pride quietly evident, "Now, relatives, friends and villagers from neighbouring areas keep coming to congratulate us. Journalists have been visiting. Our daughter has brought recognition to the family and the village. She has made the country proud."Amid all the noise, what awaits the world champion in her little corner at home?"Kadhi chaawal, her favourite, along with pointed-gourd curry and our special homemade chutney," Meena smiled. "There is one little secret, too. She loves sweetened tea, even though sugar is not ideal for athletes. I will make it for her. Home-cooked food is waiting."It takes a village, and a mother's sacrifices shaped that journey. Initially, Manisha's father, Suresh wanted her to lose weight through sport. Meena even learnt wrestling herself so she could accompany her daughter to the Nidani academy and help when sparring partners were unavailable.Nanha attended to the family's cattle as Vinod, uncle Chand Ram and cousins Jatin, Lakshya, Mohit, Priyanshu and Suryansh joined in. "Manisha was introduced to sport around 2008-09. Her late father Suresh initially enrolled her in kabaddi at the Nidani sports school near our village. She gradually developed an interest in wrestling after watching me coach," recalled Vinod."After her initial training, she moved to an academy in Samar Gopalpur village in Rohtak, run by the late coach Devilal. That was where her wrestling journey began taking shape."The mention of their father, Suresh, and the courtyard fell silent. Manisha was preparing for the 2022 Asian Championships when he passed away. She had promised him a medal. She returned with bronze.For the world championships, elder brother Rinku suggested she carry their father's photograph on her phone. Manisha wanted something more personal: a specially designed jersey featuring her father's photograph on the front and a family photograph on the back. "She wanted him with her," Meena said,.Now, as the family awaits Manisha's return, Rinku struggles to describe the transformation. "It feels as though our entire family has been reborn. People who rarely visited are coming to congratulate us. Her achievement has brought recognition to all of us," he said.It is the elder brother who has stood by her like a rock. Nobody perhaps understands the sacrifices behind Manisha's gold better than Rinku. "I accompanied her to Samar Gopalpur, where I continued playing kabaddi while she trained in wrestling. Since I had been involved in sport longer, she would discuss every little detail with me," he said.In 2017, Rinku suffered a ligament tear during a circle-kabaddi competition in Mandora village, Sonipat. Two or three surgeries followed, but his sporting career never recovered. "I had to give up kabaddi. But I made a promise to myself that whatever I could not achieve as an athlete, I would try to fulfil through Manisha. I wanted to see her become a world champion," he said.That year, Manisha joined the Sashastra Seema Bal under the sports quota and trained at Chhotu Ram Akhara in Rohtak under coach Mandeep. Eventually, she quit the job because it left insufficient time for training. A subsequent Haryana govt sports-quota appointment as a coach at the same akhara allowed her to pursue wrestling while guiding younger trainees. The pursuit came with the personal cost, that all athletes are familiar with. Today, it all seems to have borne fruit.Siwaha's narrow lanes may still confuse Google Maps. But one address needs no directions now: the home of a daughter who carried her father's promise, her brother's dreams and her village's pride all the way to the top of the world.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: UFC Vegas 123 results: Tom Nolan makes the most of controversial referee stand-up, knocks out Renato Moicano
articles.summary: After a referee restart got him out of trouble in Round 2, the 26-year-old Australian hurt Moicano with a knee and finished him with elbows in the third. It'...
articles.body:
It was UFC Fright Night for Tom Nolan, up until referee Dan Miragliotta decided to step in.

In Saturday night's UFC Vegas 123 main event, longtime UFC veteran and one-time lightweight title challenger Renato Moicano had the 26-year-old Australian in a bad position late in the second round, working with Nolan's back on the ground with a body triangle locked in. As the action slowed, Miragliotta decided to stand the fighters back up, which was essentially a "get out of jail free" card for Nolan, who took full advantage.

The 6-foot-3 Nolan landed a thunderous knee in the ensuing moments that hurt Moicano, nearly finishing him in the closing sequences of the round. It didn't take long into the third for "Big Train" to complete the job. After landing another knee, Nolan used vicious ground and pound, including massive elbows to Moicano's temple, to put the Brazilian away.

The end came at the 1:28 mark of the third round.

When asked if he was surprised that Miragliotta restarted them to standing in that second round, Nolan said he wasn't.

"Nah, I mean, you heard the crowd — they didn't love it," he said post-fight.

Then he saw a replay of his work on the big screen and was distracted by the knee that hurt Moicano.

"What a clean cross right, ohhhh," he said. "Bro, it's like we f***ing prepared for that. City Kickboxing, best gym in the world, let's go."

With the victory, Nolan (12-1) has now won six straight fights in the UFC's lightweight division, dating back to a mid-2024 stoppage of Victor Martinez. When asked what he thought of his performance, Nolan coughed up the game plan.

"We were confident the later it went, the more I'd be likely to finish him," he said. "That's why on the mat I didn't want to risk doing any stupid s*** and getting choked out. It might've been boring for you guys for like a couple of minutes, but I ended up knocking him out, so it ended up being f***ing sick."

When pressed if he'd like to call somebody out for his next fight, Nolan deferred.

"To be honest, not really," he said. "This was the guy I wanted to fight. I made a callout for the fight, and my job was to deliver tonight. This is my job right now, and I performed so, yeah — look, whatever the UFC wants to do with me next."

For Moicano (27-8-1), it's back to the drawing board after his impressive victory over Chris Duncan at the Meta Apex in April. The longtime veteran, who has two fights left on his contract, has now lost three of his last four in the UFC.

In the co-main event, Jacobe Smith showed why he believes he's the best pure wrestler in the UFC's welterweight division . Smith kept his perfect record intact by using timely takedowns, nearly nine minutes of Octagon control and strong ground-and-pound to out-point veteran Randy Brown on the scorecards.

The judges all saw it 30-27 in Smith's favor.

It's the first time the 30-year-old former collegiate All-American has gone the distance in a UFC fight, yet it was dominant from pillar to post. With the win his record improves to 14-0, while Brown, who has now lost four of his last five fights, drops to 20-9.

articles.title: Canelo vs. Mbilli winners and losers: Canelo Alvarez, Jaime Munguia salvage an event that had plenty of issues
articles.summary: Who won and lost in Riyadh on Saturday night?
articles.body:
The eyes of the boxing world were on Riyadh, Saudi Arabia on Saturday night, as Riyadh Season put on a puglistic showcase titled, "Mexico vs. the World."

On a night when Saul "Canelo" Alvarez became a three-time super middleweight champion , who were the overall winners and losers of the event?

Alvarez is a world champion again, regaining the WBC 168-pound title 13 months after losing it to Terence Crawford .

It was Christian Mbilli whom the Mexican great defeated Saturday night, winning via unanimous decision and giving us a glimpse into what Alvarez has left in the tank .

Was it vintage Alvarez? No. But after a slow start in which he seemed content sitting on the ropes, playing possum and tucking up to Mbilli's attacks, Alvarez began moving his feet, catching and countering, and punishing the Frenchman's advances with sharp riposte and some clubbing, signature left hooks.

The control came in the second half of the fight. Alvarez — like he has done to a litany of fighters — decided Mbilli couldn't hurt him and, importantly, couldn't beat him to the punch in the important exchanges. In the championship rounds, Alvarez was even able to turn the tables and become the front-foot fighter.

Is Mbilli a bona fide world-class super middleweight? Probably not, but Alvarez can only beat who is put in front of him. And looking at the current crop of super middleweight contenders, there are plenty more names — and paychecks — for the Mexican to work through on what could turn into a pre-retirement tour.

What's next for Alvarez? Well you'll have to ask Turki Alalshikh. "Canelo" still has a fight left on his contract with Saudi Arabia, so you'd imagine boxing's most influential matchmaker will want something significant and head-turning for his prized asset.

Will he find that scanning down the list of current super middleweight contenders? The WBC's interim champion is Lester Martinez. The other champions are Osleys Iglesias and Jaime Munguia, whom Alvarez already defeated. So perhaps not.

Knowing some of the curveballs that Alalshikh has thrown our way over the last couple of years, it would be a shock if he was eyeing up an all-Mexican affair between Alvarez and David Benavidez — a fight that has been on a long-running collision course, made harder in recent years by Benavidez's recent jumps in weight.

But if Alvarez can't get the dance partners, expect him to start targeting some of the arenas left on his boxing bucket list — namely, Mexico City's historic Estadio Azteca .

Munguia is fun, isn't he? They say that skills pay the bills, but entertainment sells tickets.

Munguia clung to this WBA super middleweight title, surviving scare after scare against the unheralded Nikita Zon , narrowly avoiding a huge upset after repeatedly getting hurt.

And did we witness a 2026 Round of the Year contender in Round 6 as both men traded near fight-ending blows after their own barrages of sustained attacks?

It's perhaps a damning indictment of the 168-pound landscape that Munguia finds himself sitting near the top of it. There are glaring holes in his game, but few can question his willingness to have a go. He is as game as they come and, with the title still draped over his shoulder, should make for some interesting defenses.

Bektemir Melikuziev is likely next in line. But after Saturday night, Munguia hardly looks like an immovable obstacle. There will be plenty of contenders watching the tape and fancying their chances.

But a win is a win, and Munguia wakes up on Sunday morning with a sore head as a world champion — and with a queue forming at his door.

It's sort of an unwritten rule in boxing: When you're handed a late-replacement opponent, you have to get the fighter out of there.

That's exactly what Rafael Espinoza did to Carlos Blandon in the fifth defense of his WBO featherweight crown , stopping the challenger in three rounds after the ringside doctor advised the referee to stop the fight following a cut to Blandon's left eye.

It was a sharp, well-timed right hand that did the damage to the scarred eye socket of Blandon, giving Espinoza his 29th career win alongside his 24th stoppage to stay unbeaten.

In truth, it won't be a fight that will live long in the memory. Espinoza will have been a featherweight world champion for three years once we hit December and bigger fights and harder tests are now well overdue.

The all-singing, all-dancing Espinoza said post-fight that he wants unification fights at 126 pounds, and he also wants to fight Naoya Inoue in Japan — but he didn't exactly shout it to the hilltops.

He spent more time signing to the crowd than he did giving any further details of how his 2027 might play out. And who could blame him when you have a voice like that?

Team Mexico got off to a pretty slow start on the night, rubber-stamped by the big upset of the evening as David Picasso lost via split decision to Carl Jammes Martin.

And you'd have to have a heart of stone to deny the dancing of "Wonder Boy" as he grabbed the WBC Silver featherweight title from Picasso despite suffering a knockdown in Round 7.

It was a nip-and-tuck affair across a very competitive 10 rounds. It could have gone either way on the scorecards, but Martin got the nod and extended his unbeaten professional record to 29-0 (21 KOs).

Martin has spent a majority of his career fighting in his native Philippines, but now with a recognized name on his record, he will attract a lot more attention in the 126-pound division.

I'm reluctant to lay into Mbilli too much.

DAZN's commentary team was very critical of the Frenchman's unwillingness to engage with Alvarez down the stretch, gift-wrapping his WBC world title to the man who has owned it twice before.

But it's a tale as old as time. It's easy to sit there and tell a fighter to just go for broke — but if you can't find the openings to land these bombs, then you're going to get found out with counters quickly.

"He didn't throw a lot of punches, because it's hard to throw punches with me," Alvarez said post-fight in the ring, stressing that point.

Fellow super middleweight Gabriel Rosado posted on X : "You can obviously see there's a tear on Mbilli [sic] left bicep," and perhaps some excuses will come out in the days that follow. But when Alvarez is on, you have to be pretty close to perfect to beat him.

Mbilli is only 31 years old and will rebound from this. It's the first loss of his career and he had enough moments in Saturday's fight to bolster his career-highlights package.

It's Riyadh Season, baby — and for boxing, it's a case of everybody acting like nothing is happening and nothing is wrong . It's that meme of the dog sitting having a cup of coffee while his house burns in the background.

That shouldn't be a surprise. Boxing is, after all, the black sheep of sport and often finds itself veering into its own lane, unbothered by the pile-up it leaves behind.

We knew the story heading into this weekend's card: The Iran-backed Houthi rebels of Yemen are at war with a Saudi-led coalition, and Riyadh — more specifically King Khalid International Airport — was turned into a battleground across October.

But despite the cancellation or postponement of other sporting events due to take place in Riyadh, "Mexico vs. the World" went ahead.

Alalshikh, the head honcho of Riyadh Season, was disturbingly silent.

That silence is the most telling part of all. There was very little in the way of public reassurance and little explanation of why this particular event is proceeding while others have been pulled from the calendar. Instead, the boxing machine kept rolling, seemingly determined to punch through the noise outside the ring.

And that is where the sport's peculiar relationship with Saudi Arabia becomes difficult to ignore. Boxing has spent the past few years following the money to Riyadh, happily accepting the enormous purses, grandiose production and promise of fights that once seemed impossible to make.

But when the conversation shifts from spectacle to security, the answers become harder to find.

The audience looked patchy and uninterested in Riyadh. This event alienated thousands of fans that could — and should have — witnessed an Alvarez fight live. That's if sense prevailed and Saturday's event was relocated west to the United States or perhaps Mexico.

Let's get it straight: "Bek the Bully" got screwed in October.

The dangerous Uzbek, now 30 years old, should have been fighting Jaime Munguia on this card for Munguia's WBA crown at 168 pounds, but instead Melikuziev got ignored by the champion and the sanctioning body.

Munguia was ordered to face No. 1 contender Melikuziev next, with the WBA giving both camps until Oct. 21 to reach an agreement — but the champion and his team refused, opting to invite Zon to Riyadh instead to challenge for the title.

The WBA claimed to have not approved the fight and promised to "review the situation," but in typical sanctioning body style, it stayed quiet afterward, leaving it until fight week for the chips to fall.

According to Mike Coppinger on the DAZN broadcast, Melikuziev's team accepted a step-aside deal late this week, on the condition that Melikuziev faces Munguia within the next 90 days. The agreement also includes a 60-40 purse split in favor of the champion.

After weeks of administrative limbo, it seems we've found a resolution. But would anyone really be surprised if this fight fell through again?

And considering Munguia's shortcomings against Zon on the night, Melikuziev will be going to bed tonight convinced he would have finished the job that the Russian was able to start.

After Espinoza stopped Blandon, we headed back into the DAZN studios to find Chris Mannix describing the stoppage as "extremely premature."

Now, I am no doctor. And I'm pretty sure Chris Mannix isn't a doctor, either.

But I do know who is a doctor. And that's Neil Scott, the chief medical officer of the British Boxing Board of Control from 2017 up until June of this year. Scott is still on the British Boxing Board of Control medical panel and independently contracted by the sport's leading promoters.

"I wonder what the doctor was looking at," Mannix continued. "How much experience does that doctor have in professional boxing? Because that is not the kind of cut that is deep enough to stop any fight, let alone a championship fight."

Scott's judgment should be trusted by fighters who put their lives on the line.

I get it: Mannix is paid to give his opinion. But Scott is paid to look after the health and safety of boxers — and I know which I deem more important.

Say what you want about Zuffa Boxing and Dana White — and believe me, I have — but there were moments Saturday when you couldn't help wishing their production team had been handed the keys.

White has made no secret of his desire to bring some UFC-style urgency to boxing broadcasts. That means cutting out the seemingly endless gaps between fights, ditching the unnecessary filler and, above all, keeping the action moving.

After watching fewer than five rounds of boxing across two-and-a-half hours of the broadcast before Munguia vs. Zon, you can understand the appeal.

To be fair, Kate Scott, Malik Scott and Mannix deserve some credit for keeping the conversation ticking over during the lengthy wait. They had an arena full of super middleweights to call upon for interviews, at least, as everyone patiently waited for — and I quote — "Turki Alalshikh to take his seat."

A novel reason to keep a boxing audience waiting, if nothing else.

articles.standfirst: El peleador australiano sobrevivió a las habilidades en jiu-jitsu del brasileño para finalizarlo en una cartelera llena de grandes momentos
articles.summary: El peleador australiano sobrevivió a las habilidades en jiu-jitsu del brasileño para finalizarlo en una cartelera llena de grandes momentos
articles.body: Esta pasada madrugada la UFC ha vuelto al APEX de Las Vegas con una cartelera para paladares intrépidos, donde la guinda del pastel la ha puesto Tom Nolan (12-1) al noquear a Renato Moicano (21-8-1) en el tercer asalto para dar un golpe sobre la mesa en el pelo ligero y confirmar un cambio generacional en la categoría. Nolan se estrenó en el top 15 tras superar a Fares Ziam en su última pelea, pero en esta ocasión tenía en frente la primera prueba de fuego de su carrera. De hecho, Tom reconoció antes del duelo que era admirador de Moicano, aunque el brasileño no quiso entrar en su juego de halagos e hizo gala de su famosa personalidad afirmando que él solo quiere dinero. Renato no venía a hacer amigos, y lo demostró en los dos primeros asaltos dominando en el suelo a Nolan y tomando su espalda. Sin embargo, el árbitro decidió levantar a ambos peleadores incomprensiblemente en una de esas ocasiones en las que el brasileño estaba en la espalda del australiano, lo que fue el principio del fin. Tom dañó a Moicano con una rodilla, y en el tercer asalto le finalizó con otro aluvión de golpes y ground and pound que le asegurar enfrentarse a un top 10 en su siguiente aparición. Otro de los principales protagonistas fue Jacobe Smith (14-0) en el evento co estelar, ya que dominó a Randy Brown (20-9) haciendo gala de sus habilidades en el grappling para superar con nota su primer gran reto en la división de peso wélter. Todo gran peleador debe pasar por el jamaciano en esta división, y el estadounidense le dio un correctivo a pesar de ver frenada su racha de finalizaciones en la compañía -cuatro consecutivas-. En el resto de la cartelera estelar hay que destacar la victoria de Luana Santos (12-2) ante Yana Santos (17-9, 1NC) que le deja a las puertas de una oportunidad titular en peso gallo femenino, el triunfo de todo un veterano como Cody Durden (19-11-1) ante Ode' Osbourne (13-10, 2 NC) por decisión unánime, o la actuación de Jean-Paul Lebosloyani (12-2) ante Farman Hasanov (5-1) que obligó al árbitro a parar la pelea por un aparatoso corte en el párpado del azerbayano. En las preliminares, Rodrigo Sezinando (10-2) también obligó al médico a parar su combate ante Theodor Berggren (8-5) por otro preocupante corte, mientras que Julian Erosa (32-14) se retiró de las MMA por todo lo alto con un K.O. ante JeonYeong Lee (11-4) en el primer asalto después de estar prácticamente finalizado. Además, Joe Kropschot (10-3) debutó a lo grande en la UFC con una sumisión a Nick Klein (6-4) después de ganarse su contrato en las Dana White's contender Series hace unas semanas, mientras que Lucia Szabova (13-0) también completó con éxito su primera pelea en la compañía y mantuvo su invicto tras finalizar a Tainara Lisboa (7-5) en el tercer round. articles.title: EXCLUSIVE | 'Olympics medal nahi, Olympics gold': Manisha Bhanwala's promise to her late father
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: “Bhai saab, Jind Pandavon ki nagari hai, kuch to baat to hogi [Jind is the land of the Pandavas.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: “Bhai saab, Jind Pandavon ki nagari hai, kuch to baat to hogi [Jind is the land of the Pandavas. There must be something special about it]”Manisha Bhanwala said these words with a smile a day after creating history at the World Wrestling Championships on Friday. The wrestler from Jind, Haryana, had just become the first Indian woman to win a gold medal at the World Championships.Perhaps there is something special about this town - Jind. Manisha is not the only athlete from Jind to make the country proud this year.Exactly a month earlier, another daughter of the town, Neeru Dhanda, won gold in trap shooting at the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya. She became the first Indian woman to win an individual Asian Games gold medal in trap shooting.Jind has a deep connection with the stories of the Mahabharata. According to local belief, the Pandavas built a temple dedicated to Goddess Jainti Devi before going to war against the Kauravas. They prayed to the goddess and sought her blessings for victory. The town was originally known as Jaintapuri, meaning the abode of Goddess Jainti Devi. Over time, the name became Jind.And now, Manisha has added another proud chapter to the story of this town.But for the 59kg wrestler, the biggest moment of her life was also a deeply personal one.When she won the gold medal, she did not celebrate alone. She kept the medal and a photograph of her late father beside her pillow. She made a video call to her mother and brother before going to sleep. Before kissing her father's photograph, she had one more moment with the man whose memories and teachings continue to guide her.Her father may not have been there to witness her historic achievement, but Manisha made sure he was part of it.The wrestler has often spoken about the lessons she learnt from the Bhagavad Gita through her father. She believes in the principle of karma - doing one's duty and leaving the result to God. She follows it in her life and carries the same belief onto the wrestling mat.That belief was tested in the World Championships final in Astana, Kazakhstan. Manisha was trailing American wrestler Abigail Nette by six points in the women's 59kg final. But she refused to give up. She fought back brilliantly to win 8-6 and claim the gold medal.With this victory, Manisha became the first Indian woman to win a World Championships gold medal in wrestling. She is only the second Indian overall to achieve the feat, after the legendary Sushil Kumar, who won the men's 66kg title in 2010.TimesofIndia.com spoke to Manisha from Astana about her thrilling comeback in the final, her celebration with a T-shirt carrying her father's photograph, Iranian-style wrestling, her belief in karma and her dream of winning gold at the Los Angeles Olympics.Manisha, what was going through your mind during the final? You were trailing, and then suddenly you took the lead. What did you do to turn things around? There are times in such situations when things can go either way.I was trailing. When I went to the starting point, I felt that only one point had been scored, so why were they giving that opportunity at that moment? Even then, I challenged the decision, but they still awarded the points. I objected, but my challenge was rejected. Even after that, I felt that I would be able to do it. I had that feeling.I hadn't had a good Asian Games. I was getting very frustrated. Doubts were also coming into my mind. Was I doing something wrong? This was something I asked myself when I closed my eyes for a few seconds. Was my practice wrong? Many things were going through my mind, but I believed that I could do it. I felt it from within that I could turn things around. And I did.Did you ever face a similar situation before?Yes. I faced the same situation at the 2025 Asian Championships. I was losing, but I made a comeback and won the bout.What move did you use that turned things in your favour at the Worlds?My style of wrestling is different from that of other girls. I wrestle somewhat like the Iranian style. The way I am trained is also different. For the last five years, the focus has been on being able to do anything in the first three minutes. But after that, it is about maintaining patience, stamina and strength. I also work on keeping myself mentally strong and excited. I work on all these things.If you dominate the first two to three minutes, the bout is yours. After that, it is all about your patience and analysis of the opponent. If you are trailing, you will try to score, and in most cases, you lose patience and focus, and eventually the match too.You mentioned the Iranian style. Could you explain it a little?To develop that kind of strength, like Iranian wrestlers have, a lot of force is required. I am a little shorter in comparison, so I have to work harder. First, I practise with boys. If I get injured, I may have to stay away for two days. So I try to do everything I can. Even if I have pain anywhere in my body, I complete my recovery. I spend my entire day on recovery, and only after that do I go back. I take care of my body as much as I can.What do you tell your sparring partners when you hit the mat during training?I train with multiple partners, including boys. They help me generate more force. After the selection or during camps, when it becomes clear which wrestlers will be going, we practise with those who are selected. My coach and I tell them what needs to be done and what kind of practice is required. We make a particular plan and follow it.Who is your inspiration?My father sahab. My entire life is dedicated to my father sahab. He was such a lovely soul. He was not literate. He never went to school, but always supported me throughout my journey. There were taunts like, 'Ladki hai, padha likha le, shaadi kar de.' But he never listened to them. Such was my father.I am what I am today because of him. I miss him a lot. But I still feel he is always sitting beside me. He is always there to clap for me, motivate me and cheer for me whenever I hit the mat. I feel he is always around.You took out that T-shirt with your father's photograph after winning the gold medal.As I said, he is everything to me. He was a farmer who used to plough the fields himself. We didn't have much money. But I never got to know how he fulfilled all my needs.What did he do?My father was a farmer. He used to work in the fields and operate the plough. He knew nothing about sports or anything like that. He was a farmer who never treated me differently because I was a girl. He never put any pressure on me about what I was doing or what I was eating.Even today, I feel that kind of support is rare. Despite never going to school and not being able to read or write, he was an open-minded person. He was a lovely soul. He was very particular about his work. From childhood, he taught me what karma means. He taught me the right things at that time.Our family was not financially well-off. We were very poor. We did not even have land of our own. He followed the Gita and always asked me to follow it too.How did he arrange the money? Did you ever ask him?Absolutely not. He never let me feel that I was missing anything. Let me tell you something. Even today, I don't know how my father managed everything. He worked day and night.When I started wrestling in 2015, I needed wrestling shoes. I just said once, 'Papa, wrestling ke shoes chahiye.' He kept his hand on my head with a smile and said, 'Haan, ho jayega, dikkat koi nahi hai.' He gave me shoes worth Rs 7,000 within a couple of days. Those were very expensive at that time.But from the very first day, he always made sure I got good things. He never let me feel that I was missing anything. I never asked him how he got those things, and he never told me.When I went to school, my teachers would ask me what my father did. When I told them that he was a farmer, they would sometimes find it difficult to believe that my father was a farmer.What happened to him?In 2022, when I was selected for my first championship, my father was very excited. I had beaten Sakshi Malik three times. I was doing really well. I had also defeated Sangeeta Phogat.My father started getting excited when he saw his dream beginning to come true. He was completely fine that night when I got selected for the Asian Championship. In the afternoon, he was told to go and sleep. He didn't wake up after that. He died of a heart attack. It had been eight years since then, and that very night, I had a flight for the championship.How did you support yourself that difficult night?I don't know. I was numb. I lost the person whom I loved more than anything in this world. And that person was no longer with me. That night... I don't know how to explain it. It was tough to ask myself whether I should hold on to the feeling that my father was still with me.I had a flight to the Asian Championships that same night. I just sat in a corner. After the cremation, my mother said, 'Apne papa ka dream tu poora nahi karegi toh kaun karega?' She said, 'Kya karegi aise baith ke, chal jaa, competition ladd.'I reached Mongolia from India. I did not even realise how I had travelled or how I had reached there. I don't remember that day properly. I don't remember where I was going, what day it was or what was happening around me. When I returned to my room after winning bronze, I broke down.Who all are there in your family now?My mother, my brother, my sister-in-law and my nephew.Your brother was a kabaddi player. Why did you opt for wrestling?My brother used to beat me up a lot when we were children. He used to fight with me. I was small, so I used to get beaten up and cry. My father sahab used to beat him. My father sahab said, 'Tu strong bann, pehelwaan ban, isko pitiyo bade hoke.'That's how I decided to become a wrestler.My brother also left kabaddi midway for me. He said that I should continue and that we would both do it together. He now stays at home and takes care of whatever work needs to be done. He looks after the farming. We also have a medical store there, which he manages.You train in Rohtak. Who manages those expenses?I am from Jind. I have been living in a village in Rohtak for the last 10 years. I live on rent. I have no idea how my family manages those expenses too. My father sahab and mother never told me. They always said, 'Apne khel pe dhyan do.'World Championship gold done, Asian Championships gold done, Grand Prix gold done. What next for Manisha now?Olympic gold. I will do that for my father sahab. I am confident about that. Wrestling and winning gold are the two things that remain in my life. Apne father sahab ko samarpit hai dono ab.He always used to say, 'Beta Olympics medal jitenge ek din.' Whenever he asked, I used to reply, 'Pitaji, Olympics medal nahi, Olympics gold.'Manisha, there is a shooter from Jind named Neeru Dhanda. You must have heard of her?Yes. I know her. She is from Jind itself. She won gold at the Asian Games. Jind is the land of the Pandavas. Kuch toh baat hai iski hawa mein.My father sahab was a follower of the Gita and believed in karma. He taught me to keep doing my karma. Just keep doing your work. Only God knows what you are going to receive and what you are going to get. articles.title: Canelo va a por el billón de dólares
articles.standfirst: Su acuerdo con Riyadh Season ha disparado los ingresos del boxeador mexicano y tras el combate contra Mbilli sus ganancias subirán a más de 800 millones
articles.summary: Su acuerdo con Riyadh Season ha disparado los ingresos del boxeador mexicano y tras el combate contra Mbilli sus ganancias subirán a más de 800 millones
articles.body: Canelo Álvarez acaba de derrotar a Christian Mbilli en Riad (Arabia Saudí), en una pelea que logísticamente ha sido bastante delicada por el enclave de la misma. Los ataques de las milicias hutíes de Yemen sobre la capital saudita han dejado ya más de una decena de muertos y la prudencia invitaba a llevar el evento a otro país. Sin embargo, la presencia de Canelo en Riad protagonizando un evento deportivo de dimensión mundial era importante para la imagen de normalidad que quiere proyectar el país anfitrión. En juego para Canelo estaba su legado –vuelve a ser campeón mundial del supermedio- y una bolsa astronómica. De base, el tapatío tiene garantizados 47 millones de dólares, pero la cifra se podría disparar hasta los 100 millones atendiendo a diversos pluses. Por el contrario, esta cifra contrasta con lo que recibe Mbilli, que sólo tiene 9 millones asegurados, pero también obtendrá una parte de las ganancias adicionales, según conceptos como la taquilla o las ventas de PPV. Curiosamente, la última pelea de Álvarez, aunque terminó con derrota frente a Crawfrod, le reportó unos 150 millones de dólares (de entrada tenía más de 100 garantizados). Se estima que el contrato por cuatro peleas del mexicano con Riyadh Season conlleva 400 millones garantizados. La presencia de Canelo en Riad en momentos tan difíciles para Arabia Saudí, sin duda le hará contar con el favor del promotor y ministro Turki Alalshikh, pero también era una cita que estaba pactada en dicho país y renunciar a este combate habría sido un problema contractual. Recordemos que en su día el mexicano firmó por DAZN a razón de 365 millones de dólares garantizados por 11 peleas en un periodo de 5 años, pero dicho acuerdo se finalizó de forma prematura tras la ruptura del boxeador con su promotora Golden Boy. No obstante, aquello le ha permitido al de Guadalajara firmar con diversas promociones contratos menos extensos pero más lucrativos. Según Sportico, Canelo va por 760 millones de dólares en ganancias entre bolsas de boxeo y patrocinios a lo largo de sus 20 años de carrera profesional. Muchos se cuestionan por qué Canelo sigue al pie del cañón en un oficio tan peligroso cuando además ya ha logrado tanto. De momento el riesgo parece seguir mereciendo la pena porque está ganando más dinero que nunca y continúa a buen nivel. El mexicano dice que se siente fresco y revitalizado, mejor que en mucho tiempo, después de someterse a una operación en el codo que le causó problemas durante mucho tiempo, y confirma que todavía le quedan tres o cuatro peleas. Con 36 años aún no es mayor, pero sí que es cierto que es un púgil con muchos asaltos a sus espaldas. Canelo es la última superestrella del boxeo, quien recogió la antorcha que sostenía Floyd Mayweather. Por el momento, y pese a su derrota contra Crawford, no la entrega porque vuelve a ser campeón y está batiendo récords de ganancias. Si en algún momento cruza su camino con el de algún luchador de UFC o similar, entonces sabremos que se bate en retirada. Cuando acabe su carrera, lo más probable es que el mexicano ya haya ingresado en el selecto club de los deportistas que han ganado un billón de dólares (1.000 millones) y, lo más difícil, en el de aquellos que lo han logrado mientras estuvieron en activo. La lista en estos días está compuesta, en orden de patrimonio neto, por Michael Jordan (3,5-4,7 B), Ion Tiriac (2,3-2,4 B), Tiger Woods (1,3-1,5 B), Lebron James (1,2-1,4 B), Cristiano Ronaldo (1,2-1,24 B), Magic Johnson (1,2-1,6 B), Lionel Messi (1-1,5 B), Floyd Mayweather (1,08 B), David Beckham (1 B) y Roger Federer (0,95-1,1 B)

articles.title: Canelo Alvarez regains WBC super-middleweight title with unanimous decision over Christian Mbilli
articles.summary: RIYADH, Saudi Arabia — Canelo Alvarez regained the WBC super-middleweight championship on Saturday night, using precise counterpunching and a strong second-half performance to defeat Christian Mbilli by unanimous decision.
articles.body: RIYADH, Saudi Arabia — Canelo Alvarez regained the WBC super-middleweight championship on Saturday night, using precise counterpunching and a strong second-half performance to defeat Christian Mbilli by unanimous decision. The judges scored the fight 115-112, 116-111 and 117-110 for Alvarez, who handed Mbilli his first professional defeat. Alvarez improved to 64-3-2, while Mbilli fell to 29-1-1. Returning for the first time since losing his undisputed championship to Terence Crawford in September 2025, the 36-year-old Mexican became a world champion again. The victory carried significance beyond the belt. Alvarez faced questions about whether his championship years had ended with the Crawford defeat. Against an unbeaten opponent whose pressure presented a test of his ability to sustain his work, Alvarez put together combinations and found the accuracy to take charge as the fight progressed. “Oh, it’s so difficult to explain,” Alvarez said. “It’s something unbelievable.” Mbilli’s pressure and greater activity made the opening half competitive, particularly as he pushed Alvarez toward the ropes. Alvarez answered with body punches and counters, then began finding greater success in the sixth with a right uppercut and straight right. The change was in the rhythm of the exchanges. Alvarez increasingly made Mbilli respond to his punches, interrupting the champion’s advances with cleaner shots. At times, he lowered his hands and beckoned Mbilli forward, inviting exchanges from positions where he could counter. An uppercut punctuated Alvarez’s seventh round, and he followed with combinations in the eighth. Mbilli’s task became more difficult when referee Hector Afu deducted a point for a punch to the back of Alvarez’s head. Alvarez’s jab helped him control the 10th. Mbilli continued working to the body and landed right hands in the final round, but Alvarez finished emphatically, wobbling the champion with a late right. Alvarez credited trainer Eddy Reynoso’s instructions to move, box and maintain his jab. “Do what Canelo do the best. And that’s what I did,” Alvarez said. Asked whether Mbilli surprised him, Alvarez said he expected a strong opponent but believed he had limited the champion’s offense. “It’s difficult to throw punches with me,” he said. The celebration brought an emotional tribute to Eddy Reynoso and Chepo Reynoso, whom Alvarez credited with shaping his career. Alvarez’s tearful celebration and tight embrace with Eddy Reynoso offered a different image from his composed work inside the ropes. After 12 rounds spent managing Mbilli’s pressure, he struggled to describe what becoming a champion again meant. His thanks quickly shifted from the achievement to the people who helped him reach it. “I’m so proud, so proud of my team,” Alvarez said. He also thanked his family watching from afar and joked that his wife, who could not attend, had told him not to return without the championship. “I won the title,” he said. Alvarez offered no immediate commitment to another opponent. “I’m gonna rest. I’m gonna keep learning. I’m gonna keep working hard,” he said. In the co-main event, Jaime Munguia survived a sixth-round scare to retain his WBA super-middleweight championship against Nikita Zon. Munguia won by unanimous decision, with scores of 117-111, 117-111 and 116-112, recovering after Zon hurt him to improve to 47-2. Rafael Espinoza retained his WBO featherweight title with a technical knockout of Ricardo Blandon at 1:22 of the third round. A straight right opened a cut above Blandon’s left eye, and the referee stopped the fight on the ringside physician’s recommendation. Espinoza improved to 29-0 with 25 knockouts. Reito Tsutsumi scored two second-round knockdowns before stopping Raymundo Rojas Garcia at 2:27. Tsutsumi improved to 6-0 with five knockouts.

articles.title: Sean Shelby's Shoes: What's next for Tom Nolan after UFC Vegas 123 win?
articles.summary: What does the future hold for UFC Vegas 123 main event winner Tom Nolan? We attempt to play matchmaker.
articles.body:
Tom Nolan deserves no blame for getting his hand raised against Renato Moicano at UFC Fight Night 292 , regardless of the controversy.

After being controlled on the mat for the majority of two rounds Saturday at the Meta APEX in Las Vegas, Nolan (12-1 MMA, 6-1 UFC) was the benefactor of referee Dan Miragliotta implementing a highly polarizing stand-up with Renato Moicano (21-8-1 MMA, 13-8 UFC) on his back with a body lock in.

Moments after the lightweight headliner was brought to its feet, Nolan cracked Moicano and shifted all the momentum to his side. The Brazilian barely survived the second round, then Nolan hurt him again and poured it on in the third frame, forcing the TKO stoppage .

Although his win has been overshadowed, Nolan shouldn't get heat for it. He was defending well until Miragliotta stood it up, and he showed the desperation of someone who was about to be down two rounds and put it on his opponent. Full credit to the Aussie for that.

The dust will settle from this and everyone will move on, and Nolan will be standing tall with the backing of what's now a six-fight winning streak at 155 pounds. The 26-year-old is becoming a player in one of the best divisions in the sport, and he made it clear he wants another strong test next.

Nolan mentioned Mateusz Gamrot's name after his win, and that's a perfect next step. The Polish contender is always willing to take any fight given to him, and there's no doubt he would accept Nolan if offered.

Given what Moicano was able to do in his moments of success, Gamrot (26-5 MMA, 9-5 UFC) has to feel good about his chances to repeat that. And with a different referee, too.

Nevertheless, Nolan is now part of the next wave of names at lightweight and his potential can't be ignored.

Robert Whittaker's light heavyweight journey continues at UFC Sydney.

The promotion announced Thursday that the former UFC middleweight champion is set to fight Bogdan Guskov (18-4-1) on Feb. 6 at Afterpay Arena in Sydney, Australia. Whittaker (27-9) made a successful jump up to the 205-pound division this past July at UFC 329 with a third-round knockout victory over veteran Nikita Krylov. That snapped a two-fight losing streak and the 35-year-old Whittaker looks to make one more run at a title to cap off his storied career.

Guskov seeks to right the ship after his most recent fight ended in disaster. "Hitman" was scheduled to rematch Jan Blachowicz at UFC Serbia, but instead competed a week earlier at UFC Abu Dhabi in July, stepping in as a replacement for Khalil Rountree Jr to face Magomed Ankalaev. articles.title: A wall of champions at Sir Chhotu Ram Akhara & a new name waits to join legends
articles.summary: ROHTAK: Some walls tell stories that words struggle to capture.
articles.body: ROHTAK: Some walls tell stories that words struggle to capture. Inside the wrestling academy at Sir Chhotu Ram Akhara here, one such wall speaks of Olympic glory, world-class grit and the extraordinary journeys of wrestlers who once dared to dream big. Large photographs of Sushil Kumar, Yogeshwar Dutt and Sakshi Malik adorn it, turning the space into something of an informal hall of fame. And now, there is a new champion whose photograph is waiting to find its place among these illustrious names -- Manisha Bhanwala.As you looked at the photographs, chief coach Mandeep Singh needed little prompting to guess the question. "Yes, yes, Manisha's photograph will soon be up here too," he replied to an unasked question with a smile. "These photographs are reserved for our Indian wrestling's extraordinary champions. You have to achieve something big to earn a place on this wall. When world champion Manisha returns to the academy, she will put up her own photograph. All the trainees will be here for that moment. Perhaps, the next time you visit, you will find her photo there," he said with unmistakable pride.It was an evening on Saturday when the day's gruelling training had already drawn to a close. The mats had witnessed their share of sweat, exhaustion and fierce contests, and the young wrestlers were preparing to head home. Yet, wanting to talk about Manisha gave them a reason to linger. They stayed back, eager to talk about their Manisha didi -- not merely the wrestler who had conquered the world, but the senior teammate whose training sessions they have observed, whose techniques they try to emulate and whose journey has made their own ambitions seem a little less distant.For this is no ordinary celebration at the Akhara. In winning the 59kg title at the senior world wrestling championships in Astana, Manisha has added another glorious chapter to an institution that has, over the years, quietly built a formidable reputation as a nursery for producing India's finest women wrestlers.For Mandeep, who has coached here since 2010, Manisha's triumph is the culmination of years of discipline. "When she joined me some years ago, Manisha was regular, dedicated and always looking to improve. She would identify her shortcomings and work on them. Her ground game, once a weakness, improved considerably," he said.The Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, where Manisha missed a medal, did not derail her. "After she returned, she did not miss a single day of practice. Her enthusiasm remained the same. Her only aim was to give her best on the mat," Mandeep said. Manisha now gives back to her institution as well. Posted here as a Haryana govt coach under sports quota, she guides younger wrestlers while pursuing her own career.Komal, a 65kg wrestler and Manisha's sparring partner for two years, knows the demands first-hand. They train together two or three times a week. "She is powerful, but she also points out our mistakes and tells us how to correct them. We learn a lot from her," Komal said. Even when Manisha trailed 0-6 in the world final, Komal believed she would fight back. The 8-6 comeback made the celebration sweeter.Deepanshi Phogat, a 50kg wrestler who has trained here for five years, values Manisha's generosity. "When we struggle with a move or strength, she explains it like an elder sister. She teaches from the heart," she said. For Mahi Singh, a trainee since a year, Manisha has made a world title feel within reach. "I watch her techniques and ask how to do them. I want to become a wrestler like didi and win an Olympic medal," she said.The academy's story is also one of persistence. Named after reformer Sir Chhotu Ram, it was once a male-only preserve. In the early 2000s, coach Ishwar Singh Dahiya began training girls despite social resistance. Sakshi's 2016 Rio Olympic bronze brought national recognition and helped transform the modest tin-roofed facility into a modern, air-conditioned training hall."We give the children as much time as we can. If wrestling is helping build their future, we must give them our maximum," Mandeep said. The space on wall is awaiting Manisha's photograph. On the mats, another generation is dreaming of earning place beside her.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Stipe Miocic Recalls UFC 241 Eye Injury While Praising Tom Aspinall for Vacating Heavyweight Title
articles.summary: Stipe Miocic backs Tom Aspinall's decision to vacate the heavyweight title, recalling how an eye injury and torn retina affected his own UFC career.
articles.body:
The UFC heavyweight division has been left in a difficult spot since Tom Aspinall vacated his undisputed title in September. The Englishman announced on social media that another injury to his right eye during training had disrupted his recovery, leaving his return timeline uncertain.

Aspinall hasn't competed since October 2025, when his heavyweight title fight against Ciryl Gane ended in a no-contest following a series of eye pokes. The 32-year-old later revealed that he had already agreed to a date for his next fight before suffering another setback involving the same eye. Unfortunately, the latest injury means he will have to spend even more time away from the Octagon.

The Englishman was originally expected to headline UFC 334 against Gane in a heavyweight title unification bout. However, his latest injury forced the promotion to change its plans. Gane has since been elevated to undisputed champion and is now scheduled to defend the belt against Josh Hokit.

As for Aspinall, his next major update is expected to come in January 2027, when he revisits his doctor for another assessment. If the eye hasn't recovered as hoped, he could require another operation. That would mark his third surgery on the right eye and fourth overall.

Amid the uncertainty, former two-time heavyweight champion Stipe Miocic has praised Aspinall for making the difficult decision to vacate his title rather than keep the division waiting.

Stipe Miocic Backs Tom Aspinall's Heavyweight Title Exit For Full Recovery

Speaking to Casino.org, Miocic shared his thoughts on the situation and said, "Looking at Tommy's situation, I just think, 'Good of him to do that. I understand it's probably hard for him to vacate his title the way he did. I give him kudos for doing that because I know it's hard for him."

Miocic also related to Aspinall's situation, having dealt with his own eye injury following an accidental poke from Daniel Cormier at UFC 241 . That night, Miocic knocked out the Hall of Famer to reclaim the heavyweight championship he had lost at UFC 226.

Reflecting on the experience, he added, "He was on top of the world, and then everything changed. He got an eye poke. I've been there. I've torn my retina before, and it's tough. I just want to give him lots of credit for doing that."

The former champion then recalled how the injury affected him after his second fight with Cormier. He said, "It happened to me in my second fight with DC (Cormier). I got poked in the eye accidentally, and after the fight, I was kind of like, 'Man, my eyes are kind of weird-looking and feeling weird.' Unfortunately, these things happen, but he just has to move on from it and just see it as bad luck."

Miocic also had a message for the UFC, suggesting that Aspinall shouldn't worry about the promotion's reaction to his decision. He said, "The UFC's never happy with anyone unless they're making them a ton of money, so forget about them.

He further explained why he believes vacating the championship was the right move, adding, "I think he did the right thing if you know you're going to be out that long. I've been out for a while, but I've been back within the year. If it was any longer than that, I would probably do the same as he did and vacate."

Aspinall's extended absence has also put to rest much of the speculation surrounding the seriousness of his injuries following UFC 321 in October 2025. There is still no clear timeline for when the Manchester native will be cleared to fight again, but he will likely be keeping an eye on Gane's upcoming title defense against Hokit at UFC 334.

A successful title defense for the Frenchman could keep a potential rematch with Aspinall on the table once the former champion is healthy enough to return.

articles.title: Da’Mazion Vanhouter: America's next great heavyweight? 'They can stop looking. Because I’m already here!'
articles.summary: America is searching for its next great heavyweight - and Da’Mazion Vanhouter is determined to answer the call; "I'm here for it!" he says; Watch Vanhouter on the undercard of Chris Billam-Smith vs Cheavon Clarke on Saturday, live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
Vanhouter is in the early stage of his professional career but the prospect has been blasting through his recent opposition.

An explosive puncher, he's on a run of seven consecutive inside-the-distance victories. Overall nine of his 10 stoppage wins have come in the first round.

His last fight caught the eye especially. Against the six foot eight inches tall Raphael Akpejiori in Las Vegas, it looked like Vanhouter's left shoulder was badly wrenched out of position. He responded immediately - viciously knocing Akpejiori out with his other hand.

"It was just in the moment a very sharp pain, how my shoulder was angled," he told Sky Sports . "It wasn't too crazy.

"I'm just here to fight and showcase my skills."

Vanhouter is still only 21 years old and 13 fights into a professional career that began when he was just 17. As a teenager remarkably he boxed down at super-welterweight. He's put on nearly 80lbs since then as he's developed into a heavyweight.

"I've grown into my frame but I still fight the same, the same movement, the same speed, I think I've gotten faster and obviously I hit harder now than I did before," Vanhouter said.

America was once the home of heavyweight boxing. Over the last decade, with the exception of Deontay Wilder, European fighters have dominated the heavyweight division. It's prompted a search to find America's next great heavyweight.

"They already stopped looking. Because I'm already here," he said with a beaming smile. "I'm here for it. That's the role I've taken, it's normal.

"I wouldn't be boxing if I didn't want to be the best. That means I want to be the best heavyweight."

High expectation can lead to a harsh fall. Moses Itauma, only 21 years old too, was, and is, the next great hope in British heavyweight boxing.

But even Itauma came unstuck in his first world title fight, losing surprisingly to Filip Hrgovic.

"You just can't rush the journey. It just wasn't his time and he just wasn't prepared for what happened," Vanhouter reflected.

The next step in Vanhouter's journey is a scheduled eight rounder against Ivan Balaz at the Copper Box Arena in London this Saturday, live on Sky Sports .

It's the American's fourth fight with Dana White's high-profile Zuffa Boxing promotion.

White believes that in Vanhouter they have a star for the future. "It would be great to have an unbelievable American heavyweight," White told Sky Sports .

"What America definitely needs is some heavyweights. Obviously we're high on him, we believe in him and that's exactly what we need for boxing in America."

Watch Vanhouter on the undercard of Chris Billam-Smith vs Cheavon Clarke on Saturday, live on Sky Sports .
